note: Draft proposals only (AGENTS.md 3.10): every rule needs expert approval before use. cautionFraction 0.3 and avoidFraction 0.6 are team heuristics chosen by the card (a single serving providing 30 or 60 percent of the daily limit), not from any source. Sources opened on 2026-11-11: National Dietary Guidelines for Bangladesh 2025 (142-page PDF; note its register entry is still unverified because the automated check could not confirm the title from the fetched bytes - a human should re-run check-sources), WHO Guideline: sodium intake for adults and children (2012), WHO Guideline: sugars intake for adults and children (2015). Skipped nutrients: sugars_g (WHO 2015 and BD Guideline 4 state percentages of energy only, plus a teaspoon equivalent; the only gram figure, Table 3 p.7 sugar 20 g, is a general desirable intake, not condition-specific - converting a percentage or a teaspoon myself is forbidden by the card); sat_fat_g (BD states percentages only: <10 percent of energy, Guideline 2 p.19, <7 percent for coronary heart disease, Guideline 6 p.79; the WHO 2023 saturated-fat guidance is also percentage-based). Conditions with no rules: gastric (the opened guidelines have no gastric/gastritis chapter).

rules.basis: National Dietary Guidelines for Bangladesh 2025, Guideline 2 (diabetes mellitus), p.69: for type-2 diabetes, sodium restriction varies with health status, usually in the range below 2000 mg/day.

National Dietary Guidelines for Bangladesh 2025, Guideline 7 (hypertension), p.81: consume sodium below 1.5 g (with fibre 30 g, cholesterol 150 mg); reduce salt intake to less than 1 tsp/day, preferably three-quarters of a teaspoon.

National Dietary Guidelines for Bangladesh 2025, Guideline 2, p.68-69: restrict foods containing fat and oil as people with diabetes are at higher risk of coronary heart disease, and prefer low-fat methods such as boiling, steaming and grilling.

National Dietary Guidelines for Bangladesh 2025, Guideline 2 (fats and oils), p.19: limit the intake of deep-fried foods and oily snacks; trans fats in fried and processed foods increase the risk of coronary heart disease.
